history.title: Ten Thousand Steps — the shorter boss
aliases: 10,000 Steps a Day for 30 Days... Was It Worth It?
He Chased 10,000 Steps... and Missed What Mattered
history.premise: Marcus lets his 10,000-step wristwatch target displace dinner and time with his daughter; he moves walking into errands and school trips. A coin jar explains that small amounts of activity count; he follows his daughter instead of the counter.
history.lesson: A universal 10,000-step threshold is not a magic switch; make everyday movement fit real life.

history.title: Missed One Workout? Don’t Throw Away the Month
history.premise: Marcus treats a missed workout as a ruined month. A neighbour’s unfinished brick wall shows him that earlier work remains; he returns to his routine and uses a brick as a calendar paperweight.
history.lesson: One missed opportunity need not erase habit progress; returning to a familiar routine matters more than a flawless streak.

history.title: "I'll Start Monday": The 14-Week Trap
history.premise: Marcus waits 14 weeks for the ideal Monday to start his workout routine; minor friction prompts repeated postponements. Seeing his neighbour start a cold, coughing truck anyway teaches him that action does not require a clean slate; he drops to his living room rug on Thursday in socks.
history.lesson: Waiting for a symbolic temporal landmark like Monday is often a polished excuse to delay effort; lowering immediate friction on any arbitrary day creates momentum.
notes: Distinct procrastination / fresh start effect story; no step counter or brick wall analogy.

history.title: Where Did 10,000 Steps Actually Come From?
aliases: Where Did 10,000 Steps Actually Come From?
history.premise: Marcus paces in circles around his living room late at night trying to hit 10,000 steps. A historical flashback to 1965 Tokyo reveals the number originated from the Yamasa Clock "Manpo-kei" pedometer marketing campaign ahead of the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, chosen because the kanji 万 looks like a person walking. Modern peer-reviewed studies from Harvard (JAMA Internal Medicine 2019) and The Lancet Public Health (2022) prove mortality benefits plateau near 7,500 steps, showing that sacrificing sleep for arbitrary late-night step counts is counterproductive.
history.lesson: The 10,000-step benchmark was born as a 1965 marketing slogan, not a biological threshold. Longevity benefits level off around 7,500 steps; consistency and sleep recovery outweigh hitting an arbitrary round number.
notes: Origin myth-busting story distinct from Ten Thousand Steps (2026-11-02), which was about life balance / pacing during family time.
